item.title: How far is everything? Walking London’s 15-minute city
item.dc:creator: Eriola Trungu Impersimi
item.description:
The “15-minute city” is the idea that the things you need every day should be a short walk or bike ride from home. It is usually mapped with circles: draw 1.2 km around a GP surgery and call everything inside “15 minutes away”.

People don’t walk in circles. They walk along streets, around railway lines and rivers, and over the few places where a main road can be crossed. After my pedestrian safety project I already had London’s streets on my laptop, so I asked the question properly: how far is everything on foot, along the routes people can actually take?

Six everyday services

I picked six things most households need within walking distance: a GP surgery, a pharmacy, a primary school, a food shop, a park of at least 2 hectares and a rail, Tube or tram station.

  • Streets and paths: OpenStreetMap, including footpaths, alleys and paths through parks, not just roads a car can use. Private paths and motorways are left out.
  • Services: OpenStreetMap, and the Department for Education’s register for open primary schools.
  • People: ONS small areas, with population and the English Indices of Deprivation 2025.

I placed a “home” every 50 m along every residential and main street in London, 454,115 of them, and measured the walk from each one to the nearest of each service. One shortest-path calculation per service covers the whole city. At 4.8 km/h, the usual planning assumption, 15 minutes is 1,200 m.

58% of Londoners live within a 15-minute walk of all six. That leaves around 3.7 million people for whom at least one of them is further away. Allow 20 minutes and it rises to 79%; cut it to 10 and it falls to 23%.

Service Within a 15-minute walk Within 1.2 km as the crow flies Walking more slowly (3.6 km/h)
GP surgery 79% 90% 64%
Pharmacy 88% 96% 75%
Primary school 96% 100% 87%
Food shop 98% 100% 94%
Park (2 ha or more) 97% 100% 90%
Rail, Tube or tram station 73% 87% 56%
All six 58% 32%

Food shops, parks and primary schools are almost everywhere. The gaps are stations and GP surgeries: around a quarter of Londoners are more than 15 minutes’ walk from a station, and a fifth from a GP.

Lesson one: circles flatter the city

The straight-line column is always the higher one. Among Londoners who live within 1.2 km of a station as the crow flies, 16% are still more than a 15-minute walk away; for GPs it is 12%. Across all six services, the typical walk is 1.33 times the straight-line distance.

This matters beyond this map. Plenty of planning rules are drawn as circles, such as hot-food takeaway exclusion zones around schools. A circle can take in streets that are a long way round on foot and leave out ones that are close.

Lesson two: it isn’t the poorest areas that miss out

This one surprised me. The most deprived areas do better: 68% of people in England’s most deprived tenth of areas have all six within a 15-minute walk, against 37% in the least deprived tenth. Every decile in between sits between 53% and 63%, so the real outlier is the least deprived end.

In London, deprivation is concentrated in dense inner neighbourhoods where services cluster, while many of the least deprived areas are outer suburbs laid out around the car. Their residents are also more likely to have one. Closeness isn’t the same as access, though: a GP surgery ten minutes away doesn’t help if its list is full.

Geography explains far more. In Inner London 83% of people have all six within 15 minutes; in Outer London it is 42%. The top boroughs are Islington (99%), Hackney (96%) and Westminster (94%). At the bottom are Hillingdon (10%), Havering (20%) and Bexley (23%), all big outer boroughs where stations and GPs are spread thinly. Part of Hillingdon’s very low GP figure may be OpenStreetMap missing some surgeries, which is the first thing I’ll check against the NHS list of practices.

Lesson three: 15 minutes for whom?

The 4.8 km/h figure describes a healthy adult. At 3.6 km/h, closer to an older person, a parent with a pushchair or a young child, the share within 15 minutes of all six falls from 58% to 32%. In the least deprived tenth of areas it falls to just 13%.

The people who rely most on walking are the ones a 15-minute city built around an average walker reaches least.

Try your own front door

The dashboard colours London by how many of the six are within reach, at your choice of pace and time. Click any spot, or type a postcode, and it walks outwards along the streets in your browser, showing how far you get in 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes and the route to the nearest of each service, with the walking and straight-line distances side by side.

What this doesn’t tell you

  • Nearest isn’t always usable. A GP list can be closed to new patients, a park locked at night, a station without step-free access.
  • OpenStreetMap is very good in London but not perfect. A missing footpath makes a walk look longer; a missing surgery makes it look further away.
  • The edge of London. Services just over the boundary aren’t counted, so some homes near the edge look worse off than they are.
  • Homes are points along streets, not addresses. Using every address (UPRN) is the obvious next step.

Then and now

My pedestrian project used OSMnx and Overpass to get the street network. This time the walking network is built directly from the OpenStreetMap file, footpaths and all, and the shortest-path search is a few lines of SciPy, run once per service from every location at the same time. The whole of London takes minutes on a laptop.

As before, I worked with an AI assistant, Claude. The questions and the judgement about what the numbers mean are mine. The code was tested on a made-up town where every answer can be worked out by hand, including a private shortcut it must ignore, before I trusted it with London.

What’s next

Three things. Using address points (UPRNs) instead of street points for homes. Turning the takeaway exclusion zones in my Takeaways Near Schools tool into real walking distances. And running the same code on other cities, since nothing in it is specific to London.

  • Explore the dashboard: etymo.co.uk/london-15-minute
  • Code and method: github.com/eritrouib/london-15-minute

Data: OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL); Department for Education, ONS and MHCLG (Open Government Licence). Walking times assume a constant pace and ignore waiting at crossings, hills and steps, so real walks are a little longer.

item.title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
item.dc:creator: Eriola Trungu Impersimi
item.description:
In 2021 I finished my master’s thesis in Geoinformatics at the National Technical University of Athens. It looked at 1,318 pedestrian collisions in the Municipality of Athens between 2008 and 2017 and asked a simple question: how does the shape of the city relate to where pedestrians are injured?

I found persistent hotspots in the centre, around Omonia, Syggrou and Vasilissis Sofias, and associations with bars and pubs, crossings, traffic signals and bus stops. The thesis ended, as theses do, with a list of things I wished I’d had: time of day, the age of the people involved, socio-economic context, a sense of how busy each place is.

Five years later, I asked the same questions of London. This time I had all of those things.

The data

London is a gift for this kind of work, because almost everything is open:

  • Collisions: the Department for Transport’s STATS19 data. Every police-recorded injury collision, with location, date, time, severity and the age of each casualty.
  • Neighbourhoods: ONS small-area boundaries, the English Indices of Deprivation 2025 and population figures.
  • Streets: OpenStreetMap for crossings, signals, bus stops, stations, schools, pubs and the drivable street network.

From 2021 to 2025 there were 22,108 pedestrian casualties in Greater London. 5,926 of them were killed or seriously injured, and deaths ranged from 36 to 61 a year.

Year Killed Seriously injured Slightly injured Total
2021 36 926 2,878 3,840
2022 42 1,194 3,322 4,558
2023 53 1,223 3,279 4,555
2024 61 1,136 3,254 4,451
2025 51 1,204 3,449 4,704

The low 2021 figure is almost certainly the early-2021 lockdown keeping people off the streets, a reminder that counts always carry the conditions they were collected in.

Lesson one: the denominator changes the story

Ranked by fatal and serious casualties per 100,000 residents, the City of London comes out at 167.6 a year, nearly four times the next borough, Westminster (43.0). Taken at face value, it is by far the most dangerous place to walk in the capital.

It isn’t. Only a few thousand people live in the City, while hundreds of thousands work there or pass through every weekday. Dividing by residents measures something, but not the risk of walking there. Ranked per kilometre of road instead, the order changes substantially.

Lesson two: crossings “correlate” with casualties

Comparing London’s roughly 5,000 small areas, the features that rise most strongly with serious pedestrian casualties per km² were traffic signals and crossings (rank correlations of about +0.4), followed by major roads, bus stops, junctions and pubs and bars. Almost exactly what I found in Athens.

It would be easy, and wrong, to conclude that crossings are dangerous. Two things are going on:

  • Exposure. Crossings, signals, bus stops and pubs are put where lots of people meet lots of traffic. Many of these variables partly measure “how busy is this place”.
  • Reverse causality. Crossings and signals are often installed because a location had collisions. The safety measure follows the problem.

This is why the project goes on to fit a negative binomial model that accounts for how busy each area is, asking which street features still go with more casualties once activity is taken into account. That is the question my thesis couldn’t answer with the data it had.

Finding hotspots along streets, not across them

In Athens I used planar kernel density, the familiar heatmap. Its weakness in a city is that a cluster on one road “leaks” onto a parallel street across a block. For London I measured density along the street network instead: the streets are cut into 50 m pieces and each casualty’s weight spreads along the network for 250 m.

Alongside it, a Getis-Ord Gi* analysis on small areas separates statistically significant clusters from random noise, with a correction for testing thousands of areas at once.

How far is emergency care?

My Athens dashboard showed hospitals next to collisions. In London I went a step further and measured the drive time along the street network from every casualty to the nearest A&E and to the nearest of London’s four major trauma centres, where the most seriously injured are taken.

These are free-flowing times for the hospital journey, not ambulance response times, but they show clearly which parts of London are furthest from trauma care.

Then and now

In 2021 my tools were R and ArcGIS Pro, with Esri Dashboards and StoryMaps for the visuals, and the project took months.

This time I worked with an AI assistant, Claude, and went from research questions to a tested analysis pipeline and a live dashboard in a fraction of the time. The questions, the choice of methods and the judgement about what the results mean came from my research background. The AI made it possible to build and check everything much faster, including testing the model on synthetic data with known answers before trusting it on the real thing.

The whole project uses open data and open-source Python, and anyone can rerun it.

  • Explore the dashboard: etymo.co.uk/london-pedestrian-safety. Try the spotlight on a junction you know, or play the years.
  • Code and methods: github.com/eritrouib/london-pedestrian-safety

What’s next

Two things. First, publishing the Athens work properly, re-analysed with the methods developed here. Second, an AI layer for the London data, so anyone can ask a question in plain English and get an answer computed from the data, with its sources, rather than a guess.

Data: Department for Transport STATS19, ONS, MHCLG (Open Government Licence); OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). Police-recorded data under-reports minor pedestrian injuries, and associations between areas and casualties do not show cause.
